http://www.jamaicantimes.com/news/279225.text: Devesh Uttam appointed as next Ambassador to Ethiopia ANI 06 Aug 2026, 20:59 GMT+10 New Delhi [India], August 6 (ANI): Devesh Uttam has been appointed as the next Ambassador of India to Ethiopia, the Ministry of External Affairs said on Thursday. Uttam, who joined the Indian Foreign Service in 2003, is presently Ambassador of India to Lithuania, and has been appointed as the next Ambassador of India to Ethiopia. He is expected to take up the assignment shortly. As per the website of the Indian Embassy in Vilnius, Ambassador Uttam was Head of the Consular, Passport & Visa (CPV) Division in the Ministry of External Affairs, New Delhi. He was also in charge of the Office of the Central Authority for Extradition Matters. His diplomatic assignments abroad included Deputy Chief of Mission at the Embassy of India, Tehran; and Counsellor at the Permanent Mission of India to the United Nations in New York. While in New York, he was also elected to serve as a Member of the United Nations Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions (ACABQ) from 2013 to 2016. He also served as India's representative on the Advisory Board of the UN Democracy Fund during his tenure in New York. Besides, he has also served in Indian Missions in Libya and Syria. He headed the Political and Commercial wings at the Embassy of India, Tripoli and the Culture and Information wing at the Embassy of India, Damascus At the Ministry of External Affairs, besides Joint Secretary, CPV Division, he has served in different Capacities including Director (Administration) and Under Secretary / Deputy Secretary (Gulf). Before joining the Indian Foreign Service, he served as Assistant Director General of Foreign Trade in the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India. He holds Master's and M.Phil. degrees from Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi. His area of research in M.Phil. was the 'Eastern Enlargement of the European Union'. The focus of the study was the cost-benefit analysis for new Member States joining the EU. He has also studied International Business at the Indian Institute of Foreign Trade (IIFT), New Delhi. He speaks Hindi, English and Arabic. He has also studied French and Sanskrit. Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Two faculty members in Tennessee Tech University’s School of Music recently represented the university on the international stage with a performance at the 58th International Horn Symposium in Kraków, Poland. Gözde Çakır Ramsey, assistant professor of flute at Tech and principal flutist of the Tech-affiliated Bryan Symphony Orchestra, and Justin Stanley, assistant professor of horn and principal horn of the BSO, performed as the Center Hill Duo at the symposium. The International Horn Symposium, held in July at the Krzysztof Penderecki Academy of Music, brought together horn performers, teachers, students, composers and scholars from around the world. This year marked the first time the symposium was held in Central Europe. For Çakır Ramsey and Stanley, the performance marked their second consecutive appearance at the International Horn Symposium. The duo previously performed at the 57th International Horn Symposium in 2025 at James Madison University in Virginia. “We were honored to represent Tennessee Tech at such a prestigious international gathering of musicians and educators,” Çakır Ramsey said. “Performing alongside artists and scholars from around the world provided an incredible opportunity to share our music, learn from our colleagues and build meaningful connections through music.” As the Center Hill Duo, Çakır Ramsey and Stanley presented works by composers Katherine Hoover, Eric Ewazen and Georges Barboteu. The program highlighted the distinctive combination of flute and horn, an uncommon pairing in chamber music. The contrasting timbres, projection and volume of the flute and horn present unique challenges for performers, requiring careful attention to balance and blend. The duo uses those differences to explore a broad range of sounds in its performances. While in Kraków, the Center Hill Duo also collaborated with Olga Tsymbaluk, piano professor at the Krzysztof Penderecki Academy of Music. Tsymbaluk joined the duo for a performance, adding piano to the ensemble. Despite having only 45 minutes to rehearse together, the musicians were able to prepare the full program and perform successfully, thanks in part to Tsymbaluk’s musicianship and collaborative approach. The Kraków performance is only the latest artistic engagement for faculty in Tech’s School of Music, which presents more than 200 concerts and recitals each year and saw a nearly 72% enrollment increase between 2021 and 2025. Audiences can next see Çakır Ramsey and Stanley perform at the Bryan Symphony Orchestra’s free outdoor community concert Sunday, Sept. 6, in Cookeville’s Dogwood Park. Family activities and vendor stations open at 5:30 p.m., and the concert performance begins at 7 p.m. Learn more about the Tennessee Tech School of Music at www.tntech.edu/music . http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27928.text: Big News Network.com Estonian defense minister quits after wasting 70 million on faulty shells for Ukraine Tallinn made multiple advance payments to a company with no artillery ammo-making experience, receiving "useless" product after repeated delays Estonian Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur has announced his resignation after it emerged that Tallinn had paid some 70 million ($81 million) in advance for artillery shells for Ukraine to a company with no track record of producing such ammunition. The scandal erupted on Wednesday after the Eesti Ekspress newspaper reported on the botched procurement and the ensuing legal dispute. In August 2024, Tallinn signed a contract with Italian-registered Datasel, owned by Indian company Neco Defence Munitions, to supply artillery ammunition for Ukraine. The government paid 15 million upfront despite neither company having any previous record of manufacturing artillery shells. A second deal followed in October, with Estonia paying another 10 million in advance. The first batch was due to reach Ukraine in November, but Datasel reported problems and repeatedly delayed delivery. Despite the setbacks, Estonia signed two more contracts with the company, eventually bringing total advance payments to around 70 million. The money came from the EU's European Peace Facility, which has been extensively used to fund weapons and other military assistance for Kiev. Tallinn is now disputing the contracts in a case before the European Court of Arbitration in Strasbourg in a bid to get money back. The government acknowledged the blunder, with Pevkur proclaiming the readiness to take the "political responsibility" and announcing his resignation. The outgoing minister, who will stay in the role until a replacement is picked, however, appeared to shift the blame for the affair on the country's procurement authority, the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK). "The defense minister does not conduct contract negotiations. The defense minister does not count socks and ammunition. The defense minister makes the fundamental decision to support Ukraine," Pevkur explained. The RKIK boss, Elmar Vaher, acknowledged that his agency was to blame for the scandal, yet shifted responsibility to his predecessor, Magnus-Valdemar Saar. "I have been familiar with the matter since January. I cannot see inside people's heads to know how they were thinking and what the main arguments behind their decisions were," Vaher told the ERR broadcaster. "The decision was made by RKIK's former director general." It remained unclear to what extent the contracts remained unfulfilled, since Estonian officials provided conflicting accounts on the matter. Pevkur said that "tens of millions of euros' worth of the ammunition" were delivered and are currently sitting "in a warehouse in a European country." The shells, however, were "not of sufficient quality" to send them into Ukraine, according to the outgoing minister. The defense ministry's secretary general, Kaimo Kuusk, described the consignment as "wholly incomplete," while the Eesti Ekspress report called the munitions "useless" and faulty. https://www.dw.com/en/avalanche-in-nepal.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NMbF The Himalayas in Nepal are home to many peaks popular with tourist climbers from around the globe [FILE: April 17, 2026] Image: Elisa Schu/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Two people have died when an avalanche struck the base camp of a mountain in Nepal with at least 14 others still missing. The avalanche hit the 7,126-meter (23,380-foot) Himlung Himal after several days of heavy rain and snowfall across the region. The dead and missing are all mountain guides and staff of Nepalese expedition companies who had been preparing the base camp for paying customers to climb the mountain. "There were a total of 14 kitchen staff members and two climbing guides from different companies who were missing," the Nepal National Mountain Guide Association said. "The two climbing guides have been found, but sadly, both were found deceased." Unclear how many are missing There was conflicting information as to how many people were in the affected area near the border with Tibet at the time of disaster. Local police said there were at least 22 people at the base camp when the avalanche struck on Sunday morning. Bibhuti Chand Thakur, head of trekking company Himalayan Holidays Nepal, told news agency DPA that search and rescue operations were under way. "The chance of survival remains high because of fresh snow," he said, adding that he did not yet have a definitive number of missing or survivors, as the area is remote and cut off from communication. While Mount Everest (pictured) is Nepal's most famous peak, peaks like Himlung Himal are also popular with climbers [FILE: May 21, 2024] Image: Narendra Shahi Thakuri/dpa/picture alliance Authorities had warned of severe weather across Nepal over the weekend. Rain has affected much of the country since Thursday, with snowfall reported in the higher northern regions. The conditions have disrupted roads and trekking routes and led authorities to suspend climbing and trekking activities on several mountains. The Himalayan nation is home to eight of the world's 14 mountains higher than 8,000 meters, and trekking and mountaineering tourism is vital to the country's economy. The latest avalanche comes as Nepal continues to recover from devastating floods in August that killed more than 1,400 people and left thousands missing. https://www.mediafax.ro/english/alexandr.text: Alexandru Rogobete urges patients to post photos of hospital food Alexandru Rogobete maintains that hospital food remains a priority for him, emphasizing that the way meals are prepared and served in hospitals is not merely an administrative detail, but a matter of respect, dignity, and—above all—medical care. „Patient nutrition is part of the therapeutic process! Nutrition plays an essential role in recovery, the effectiveness of treatment, and the well-being of those admitted to the hospital,” the Minister of Health points out. He says he wants to learn from patients and their families what the food in Romania’s hospitals is like. „I invite you to post photos of the meals served in hospitals in the comments section and to specify the healthcare facility. I want to see the positive examples! Where the food is of good quality, well-prepared, and served under decent conditions, the managers and their teams deserve to be congratulated! But I also want to see the negative examples!” Alexandru Rogobete wrote on Facebook. He asserts that in cases where patients receive poor-quality or insufficient food, or food that is served improperly, hospital managers should sit down and eat the same meals alongside the patients. „I don’t want sugar-coated reports. I want to know the reality, directly from the people living these experiences,” the minister adds. This is not the first time Rogobete has brought up the issue of food quality in hospitals. In July 2025, the minister announced that he would sit down with the managers of various healthcare facilities and eat the same food provided to the patients. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw4g.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Kuwait condemned the attack, which Iran said targeted an airbase hosting US forces (file photo) By David Gritten Published 18 November 2026 Kuwait and Bahrain have said they repelled Iranian air attacks overnight as hostilities between Iran and the United States rise. The drone attack on Kuwait was the first in more than two months. The Iranian army said it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase, which hosts US forces, but Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage. It came after US warplanes struck an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to US military officials. Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm said a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on Tuesday. The recent exchanges of fire, as well as deadlock in negotiations on a peace deal, have raised fears of a major escalation in the nine-month-old war. The conflict began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Since then, Iran has retaliated for US and Israeli strikes by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel. It has also attacked dozens of commercial vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass. Pakistani man sentenced to 27 years for Iran-backed plot to kill Trump Published 1 day ago Trump says US taking 'very seriously' any Iranian plot against Washington Published 1 day ago Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack Published 3 days ago On Tuesday night, Kuwait's military said its air defences engaged "drone threats" but did not report any casualties or damage. The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, saying it "flagrantly violated Kuwait's sovereignty, directly threatened its security and stability, and constituted a grave breach of international law". "The explosions seemed to be coming from far away, but hearing them again after a period of calm was both surprising and worrying," Hani Mohammed, an Egyptian resident of Kuwait, told AFP news agency. Bahrain's military also said on Wednesday that its air defence systems had "intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks". The island kingdom, which hosts the US Navy's 5th Fleet, has reported four attacks over the past six days, following a two-month lull. Qatar, which has mediated in the stalled indirect talks between Iran and the US, said the Iranian attacks on its neighbours were a "dangerous escalation that threatens to complicate efforts aimed at containing tensions". The Iranian army said its drones had targeted US Patriot air defence systems and drone and missile launch platforms at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Later, the army's commander-in-chief, Maj Gen Amir Hatami, warned the US and its allies that it would respond more forcefully to any new attacks on Iran. "If the enemy repeats its mistake... we have the readiness and the plans to confront it and its supporters in a stronger, more crushing way and without geographic limitations," he said. On Tuesday night, US fighter jets targeted a missile launch site on Qeshm Island "with precision munitions" in response to Iranian "aggression targeting US personnel and assets", US military officials said. Iranian media reported explosions on the island but cited a local official as saying they had caused no damage to infrastructure. In a separate development, the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) said a search-and-rescue operation was under way for a missing sailor following an attack on one of its vessels in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. The rest of the crew were safely evacuated and 11 were receiving medical care, it added. The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre reported that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about 13 nautical miles (24km) north of Khasab, in Oman's Musandam peninsula. It said the attack caused a fire on board that was extinguished. Iran said two oil tankers and a ship carrying liquefied natural gas (LNG) had caught fire after hitting naval mines while sailing along an "authorised route". At least 25 seafarers have been killed across the Middle East since the start of the war, when the Strait of Hormuz was effectively closed due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports. The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the conflict and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters. In recent months, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling through the Strait of Hormuz, allowing crude oil exports from Gulf states to reach around 80% of pre-war levels, according to analysts.
